A close reading for the week

“was Pip”

Great Expectations · Chapter 1

A small boy in a churchyard works out, one clause at a time, what the world is and where he fits in it. The sentence saves him for last, and the moment it ends a convict rises from among the graves.

Ours was the marsh country, down by the river, within, as the river wound, twenty miles of the sea. My first most vivid and broad impression of the identity of things1 seems to me to have been gained on a memorable raw afternoon towards evening.2

  1. 1

    A child’s philosophy lesson

    “The identity of things” is an abstract phrase for a memory of early childhood, because it is not the child’s phrase. The adult Pip narrates, choosing words the boy could never have used, for an experience the boy alone had. That doubleness, a child’s terror in an adult’s syntax, runs through the whole novel and is audible in every clause here.

  2. 2

    Memory setting its scene

    “Seems to me to have been gained” is carefully hedged: the narrator admits he is reconstructing. Yet the afternoon itself is “memorable” and “raw”, felt on the skin. Dickens lets certainty and reconstruction sit in one sentence, which is what long memory feels like: vivid, and not quite verifiable.
